page_hint: Ch 9 §6 (Architecture Consequence), anchors also in §3 Option A and §6 cost paragraph
quoted_clause: keeping the all-reduce on-node gives an ideal ring time about 11× below the assumed InfiniBand case and about 180× below the assumed RoCE case (§9.3)
observed: The chapter compares an eight-rank on-node NVLink all-reduce with eight-rank cross-node InfiniBand and Ethernet all-reduces, then uses the resulting 11×/180× ratios as if they were fabric alternatives for the same data-parallel training job. The same conflation appears in the cost paragraph: 'A cluster of 8‑GPU H100 servers (NVSwitch inside each node) is the highest upfront capital expenditure, but it delivers the lowest per-iteration communication time' versus 'A cluster connected by 200 GbE RoCE has lower capital cost but higher per-iteration communication time.'
evidence: The §9.3 example explicitly says the NVLink case is 'not a memory-feasible eight-replica training deployment' and is a communication-only comparison. A data-parallel job across eight nodes with eight GPUs per node spans 64 ranks, not eight ranks inside one host. NVLink inside a node and InfiniBand/RoCE between nodes are complementary layers, not mutually exclusive alternatives. The 11×/180× ratios therefore compare different group sizes and topology scopes, not two fabrics serving the same collective.
root_cause: The chapter treats 'on-node NVLink' and 'inter-node InfiniBand/RoCE' as alternative fabrics for one all-reduce, instead of distinguishing intra-node and inter-node portions of a hierarchical collective.
correction: Rewrite §6 to separate the two layers. State that an eight-node data-parallel job uses NVLink/NVSwitch for intra-node exchanges and InfiniBand/RoCE for inter-node exchanges; compare InfiniBand versus Ethernet only for the inter-node portion, and compare NVLink only for the intra-node portion. If the chapter wants to retain the 11×/180× numbers, label them explicitly as comparisons between an eight-rank single-host collective and an eight-rank cross-host collective, not as fabric choices for the same job. Remove or qualify the capex/opex paragraph so it does not imply that NVSwitch-inside-node and 200GbE RoCE are mutually exclusive cluster designs.
acceptance_test: A reader can explain why an eight-node, eight-GPU-per-node data-parallel all-reduce uses both NVLink and InfiniBand/RoCE, and cannot infer from §6 that replacing InfiniBand with NVLink inside each node eliminates the inter-node collective.

page_hint: Ch 9 §7 first bullet ('What We Still Don't Know')
quoted_clause: The benchmark numbers above assume a dedicated collective on a quiet fabric.
observed: The chapter's §9.3 numbers are analytical estimates, not benchmark measurements. §9.3 says 'These are analytical comparisons, not measured NCCL results'; Fig 9.1 says 'No curve is measured performance.' The §7 bullet nevertheless calls them 'benchmark numbers.'
evidence: The manuscript's own evidence labels and caveats contradict the phrase 'benchmark numbers.' This is an evidence-label error, not a numerical error.
root_cause: The uncertainty bullet was written as if §9.3 contained measurements, while the chapter deliberately presents analytical comparisons.
correction: Replace 'The benchmark numbers above' with 'The analytical estimates above' or 'The communication arithmetic above.' If the bullet intends to discuss real benchmark data, add a separate sentence identifying which measured results, if any, are being referenced.
acceptance_test: No sentence in Ch 9 calls the §9.3 analytical estimates 'benchmark numbers' or otherwise implies they are measured results.

page_hint: Ch 9 §1, paragraph beginning 'The bandwidth each collective consumes...'
quoted_clause: the number of participating nodes (N)
observed: The text defines N as the number of participating nodes, but the chapter has just established that a rank is not a synonym for a server and that one server can host several ranks. The collective arithmetic in §9.3 uses N as the number of ranks in the ring, not the number of nodes.
evidence: The chapter's own definition says 'A rank is an index within a communication group, not a synonym for a server — one server can host several ranks.' The ring formula uses eight logical ranks, not eight nodes. Using 'nodes' for N creates a terminology drift that can produce wrong group-size arithmetic in multi-GPU nodes.
root_cause: The sentence uses 'nodes' where the collective model requires 'ranks' or 'participants.'
correction: Replace 'the number of participating nodes (N)' with 'the number of participating ranks (N)' or 'the number of participants in the collective (N).' Audit the surrounding paragraph and §9.3 for any other place where 'node' is used for a collective rank.
acceptance_test: Every use of N in Ch 9's collective arithmetic is explicitly a rank count or participant count, and no sentence defines N as a node count.

quoted_clause: The collective operations that dominate multi-node training and inference are:
observed: The list that follows contains all-reduce, all-gather, and reduce-scatter, but omits all-to-all. All-to-all is a dominant collective for MoE training and inference, and the chapter's own Table 9-2 includes it. The sentence therefore overstates the list's completeness.
evidence: Table 9-2 includes all-to-all and describes it as 'Redistribute a source-by-destination partition, as in expert routing.' Expert parallelism is a major multi-node training and inference pattern. A reader told that the three listed operations 'dominate' may under-budget all-to-all traffic in MoE systems.
root_cause: The list was scoped to the three collectives used in the chapter's ring arithmetic, but the sentence claims dominance across multi-node training and inference.
correction: Either add all-to-all to the list and explain its role in expert routing, or qualify the sentence: 'The three collectives used in this chapter's ring arithmetic are...' Do not claim that the list is the complete set of dominant multi-node collectives.
acceptance_test: The chapter either includes all-to-all in its 'dominant collectives' list or explicitly limits the list to the collectives used in its worked example.

quoted_clause: Measured effective bandwidth is typically 40–60% of peak [ILLUSTRATIVE]
observed: The sentence begins with PCIe Gen5 x16 but then states a general 'typically 40–60% of peak' figure without scoping it to PCIe, NVLink, InfiniBand, message size, or collective type. Modern NVLink and InfiniBand large-message collectives can achieve substantially higher fractions of peak; PCIe and small-message collectives can be lower.
evidence: The chapter itself distinguishes peak from achieved bandwidth and warns that message size and topology matter. A single 40–60% range across all fabrics is not supported by the chapter's own analysis and can mislead capacity planning.
root_cause: A PCIe-specific observation was generalized into a cross-fabric rule of thumb.
correction: Scope the range explicitly, e.g. 'For PCIe Gen5 x16 and small-to-medium collectives, measured effective bandwidth is often in the 40–60% range; NVLink and InfiniBand large-message collectives can achieve higher fractions, but must be measured.' Alternatively, remove the numeric range and keep the instruction to design against measured bandwidth.
acceptance_test: The Common Mistakes section does not state a universal 40–60% effective-bandwidth range without fabric, message-size, and collective-type qualifications.

quoted_clause: RoCE and InfiniBand use the same 64b/66b line coding but differ in framing and header sizes.
observed: The claim is overgeneralized. 200GbE and 400GbE Ethernet commonly use 256b/257b transcoding, not 64b/66b, and line coding varies by speed and PHY. InfiniBand's coding also varies by generation. The sentence presents a single coding scheme as common to both families.
evidence: The chapter is otherwise careful to distinguish standards, implementations, and physical layers. A blanket 'same 64b/66b line coding' statement collapses those distinctions and can produce incorrect payload-efficiency arithmetic at 200/400Gb/s.
root_cause: A low-speed Ethernet/InfiniBand coding detail was generalized across all current speeds.
correction: Replace the sentence with a speed-scoped statement, e.g. 'At the speeds discussed here, Ethernet and InfiniBand use different physical-layer coding and framing; use the specific standard's payload-efficiency figure rather than assuming a common 64b/66b overhead.' If the 64b/66b example is retained, label it as applying only to the specific 25/100Gb/s cases where it holds.
acceptance_test: The chapter no longer claims that RoCE and InfiniBand universally use the same 64b/66b line coding; any coding-efficiency example is tied to a specific speed and standard.

page_hint: Ch 9 §5, fourth and fifth Common Mistakes bullets
quoted_clause: the price per GB of optics and cables is 5–10× that of Ethernet [ILLUSTRATIVE] ... a 200 Gb/s RoCE2 link delivers ~180 Gb/s
observed: Two terminology/unit problems: 'price per GB of optics and cables' uses a storage-capacity unit for a cost comparison that should be per port, per cable, or per Gb/s; and 'RoCE2' is not the standard spelling of RoCEv2.
evidence: The surrounding discussion compares fabric cost and link throughput, not cost per gigabyte of stored data. 'RoCE2' appears twice in the same section and is inconsistent with the standard term 'RoCEv2.'
root_cause: Informal shorthand and a unit error survived copyediting.
correction: Replace 'price per GB of optics and cables' with 'price per port, cable, or Gb/s of optics and cables' and replace 'RoCE2' with 'RoCEv2' throughout.
acceptance_test: The cost comparison uses a dimensionally appropriate unit, and every occurrence of the protocol name is spelled 'RoCEv2.'

quoted_clause: Table 9-2 states the full set of operations this chapter's traffic arithmetic can encounter within one group.
observed: Table 9-2 includes Barrier, Reduce, Broadcast, and All-to-all, none of which appear in the chapter's traffic arithmetic. Barrier in particular has no byte-traffic arithmetic. The sentence overclaims the table's scope.
evidence: The chapter's worked example uses only reduce-scatter and all-gather within an all-reduce. Table 9-2 is a broader semantics reference, not the 'full set' encountered by the traffic arithmetic.
root_cause: The table was expanded beyond the arithmetic but the introductory sentence was not updated.
correction: Change to 'Table 9-2 summarizes the collective operations discussed in this chapter and the semantics that matter when interpreting their traffic.' Or explicitly separate the operations used in the arithmetic from the broader reference table.
acceptance_test: The sentence introducing Table 9-2 does not claim that every listed operation participates in the chapter's byte-traffic arithmetic.

page_hint: Ch 9 §8 mini-case, paragraph beginning 'Concretely, for the canonical 8×H100 host...'
quoted_clause: the meaningful per-step data movement is a TP all-reduce of the per-layer activations (tens of MBs, not GBs)
observed: The phrase 'tens of MBs' is presented without a batch-size or sequence-length assumption. For single-token decode at small batch, per-layer activation exchange can be kilobytes to low megabytes; for large batched decode it can reach tens of megabytes. The range is workload-dependent.
evidence: The chapter's own mental model makes activation size a function of batch, sequence length, hidden size, and dtype. A bare 'tens of MBs' can be misread as a property of the canonical host rather than of a particular operating point.
root_cause: A representative order-of-magnitude estimate was stated without its operating-point assumptions.
correction: Add the batch/sequence assumptions behind 'tens of MBs,' or replace with a scaling statement: 'per-layer activation exchange scales with batch × sequence length × hidden size × dtype; at the canonical operating point it is on the order of X.'
acceptance_test: The mini-case states the batch/sequence assumptions behind its activation-size estimate, or replaces the estimate with an explicit scaling relation.

page_hint: Ch 9 §8 mini-case, paragraph beginning 'In disaggregated serving...'
quoted_clause: exchanging activations or KV fragments is the normal case that fits comfortably within NVLink
observed: The 35 GB KV transfer is calculated at ~0.08 s over 450 GB/s, which is a lower bound and can be significant relative to TTFT or decode SLOs. 'Fits comfortably' is an unsupported qualitative conclusion.
evidence: The same paragraph gives the arithmetic: 35 GB ÷ 450 GB/s ≈ 0.08 s. Whether that is 'comfortable' depends on the SLO, the transfer path, and whether the transfer is on the critical path. The chapter elsewhere insists on measured paths and SLO-goodput.
root_cause: A bandwidth-feasibility statement was phrased as a latency-comfort statement.
correction: Replace 'fits comfortably within NVLink' with 'is bandwidth-feasible on NVLink in this idealized calculation; whether 0.08 s is acceptable depends on the TTFT/SLO budget and the measured transfer path.'
acceptance_test: The mini-case does not assert that a ~0.08 s KV transfer is 'comfortable' without tying that judgment to an explicit SLO or measured path.

quoted_clause: prefill is **compute-bound** ... decode is **bandwidth-bound**
observed: The text states the regimes as general properties of prefill and decode, not as first-order regimes for the canonical workload. The same unqualified framing recurs in the P/D definition, mental model, disaggregation section, and speculative-decoding common mistake.
evidence: Prefill can be memory- or communication-bound at short sequences, small batches, or low arithmetic intensity; decode can be compute-bound at large batch, long context, or high arithmetic intensity. The book's own roofline model requires model architecture, sequence length, batch/concurrency, precision, kernels, hardware, and serving configuration.
root_cause: A useful first-order regime was promoted to a universal law; the canonical workload's assumptions were dropped.
correction: Qualify every occurrence: 'for the canonical 9.2K/300 workload on 8×H100 with FP16 and the stated batch, prefill is compute-dominated and decode is bandwidth-dominated; this is a regime, not a law.' Add the conditions and a counterexample.
acceptance_test: Search all occurrences of 'prefill is compute-bound' and 'decode is bandwidth-bound'; each is either scoped to the canonical workload or accompanied by the conditions under which it fails. No unqualified universal remains.

quoted_clause: TTFT budget 1.2 s ... inflating TTFT toward the 2 s SLO breach
observed: The canonical workload sets a 1.2 s TTFT budget, but the discrete-batching paragraph compares TTFT to a 2 s SLO. If 2 s is an end-to-end SLO, the sentence conflates TTFT with end-to-end latency; if 2 s is the TTFT SLO, the 1.2 s budget is stale.
evidence: The two values are in the same worked example; no definition distinguishes them.
root_cause: Canonical SLO ledger not reconciled; TTFT and end-to-end latency mixed.
correction: State the canonical SLOs explicitly: TTFT ≤ 1.2 s, TPOT ≤ 25 ms, end-to-end ≤ 2 s (if that is the intent). Rewrite the discrete-batching sentence to use the correct metric and value.
acceptance_test: A single canonical SLO table lists TTFT, TPOT, and end-to-end; every worked example uses those values and names the metric.

quoted_clause: ideal utilization is ... ≈ 2.9× (out of 4×)
observed: 2.9× is an ideal speedup, not utilization. Utilization is 2.9/4 = 72.7% (or 32/44 = 72.7%). The same mislabel appears for 3.66×.
evidence: Formula gives speedup mP/(m+P−1); utilization = m/(m+P−1). For P=4,m=8, utilization = 8/11 = 72.7%, speedup = 32/11 = 2.91×.
root_cause: Speedup and utilization conflated.
correction: Call 32/11 an ideal speedup; report utilization separately as 8/11 ≈ 72.7% (or 32/44). Do the same for m=32: speedup 128/35 ≈ 3.66×, utilization 32/35 ≈ 91.4%.
acceptance_test: Every PP example labels speedup and utilization separately and the arithmetic matches the definitions.

quoted_clause: so P−1 stage-slots are wasted out of the m · P slots each stage would otherwise work
observed: The formula is correct, but the explanation is dimensionally wrong. The pipeline adds P−1 time slots to the makespan; each of P stages is idle for P−1 slots, so total idle stage-slots are P(P−1), not P−1. The bubble fraction of makespan is (P−1)/(m+P−1).
evidence: For P=4,m=8: makespan = 11 slots; each stage works 8, idle 3; total idle = 12 stage-slots; total capacity = 44; utilization = 32/44 = 72.7%.
root_cause: Time slots and stage-slots conflated.
correction: Rewrite: 'The pipeline makespan is m+P−1 stage-times instead of mP; the bubble is P−1 stage-times per stage, so utilization is m/(m+P−1).'
acceptance_test: The derivation of the bubble fraction and total idle stage-slots matches the formula.

quoted_clause: ~1.29 PFLOP → ~1.19 PFLOPS required over the ~1.08 s prefill budget, vs 0.989 PFLOPS peak
observed: 1.29/1.08 = 1.194 PFLOPS is the aggregate rate for one request. Comparing it to 0.989 PFLOPS (one H100's FP16 dense peak) is only valid if the request is served by one GPU. The canonical host is 8×H100 with aggregate peak ~7.91 PFLOPS; per-GPU required rate is ~0.149 PFLOPS. The sentence does not state which denominator is intended.
evidence: 8 × 0.989 = 7.912 PFLOPS. 1.194/8 = 0.149 PFLOPS per GPU. At 10 rps, aggregate prefill demand is 12.9 PFLOPS, which exceeds the node peak; that is the relevant capacity statement.
root_cause: Aggregate vs per-GPU vs per-node throughput mixed; concurrency omitted.
correction: State the basis explicitly: per request, 1.29 PFLOP over 1.08 s = 1.19 PFLOPS aggregate; on 8×H100 that is 0.149 PFLOPS/GPU vs 0.989 peak; at 10 rps the aggregate is 12.9 PFLOPS, so one node cannot sustain the canonical average without more replicas. Use the correct denominator for the claim.
acceptance_test: A dimensional ledger shows per-request FLOPs, per-request rate, per-GPU rate, per-node peak, and offered load; every comparison uses matching units and scope.

quoted_clause: the shard-invariant cause is the low ~1.0 FLOP/byte intensity
observed: The ~1.0 FLOP/byte figure is the batch-size-1 decode intensity for FP16 weights (2 FLOPs per parameter per token / 2 bytes per parameter). At the canonical continuous-batching concurrency, intensity is B × 1.0 FLOP/byte (before KV/attention traffic), so at B=16 it is ~16 FLOP/byte, not ~1.0. The text does not state the batch assumption.
evidence: Arithmetic intensity = 2B / bytes_per_param. For FP16, = B FLOP/byte. The H100 FP16 ridge point is ~989 TFLOPS / 3.35 TB/s ≈ 295 FLOP/byte, so decode can still be bandwidth-bound at B=16, but the stated 1.0 is not the serving operating point.
root_cause: Batch-size-1 roofline number used as a shard-invariant serving property.
correction: Write the batch-dependent formula, state the canonical batch/concurrency, and compute the actual intensity. Say 'at batch 1, ~1 FLOP/byte; at the canonical batch B, ~B FLOP/byte; still below the ridge point, so bandwidth-dominated, but not 1.0.'
acceptance_test: The roofline calculation includes batch size and matches the canonical serving concurrency; no unqualified 1.0 FLOP/byte claim remains.

quoted_clause: PagedAttention improves memory capacity by eliminating KV fragmentation.
observed: PagedAttention reduces external fragmentation and over-reservation by allocating fixed-size blocks; it does not eliminate fragmentation. Block-level internal fragmentation remains, and metadata/page-table overhead exists. It improves effective capacity utilization, not physical capacity.
evidence: Fixed-size blocks can waste up to block_size−1 slots per allocation; the book's own [S6] note says block-allocation/metadata overhead is not vendor-measured.
root_cause: Mechanism overstated as elimination.
correction: Say 'reduces external fragmentation and over-reservation, improving effective KV capacity; block-level internal fragmentation and metadata overhead remain.'
acceptance_test: No 'eliminating fragmentation' claim; the text distinguishes external vs internal fragmentation and capacity vs utilization.

quoted_clause: Prefix caching reduces memory capacity and prefill compute by reusing already-computed KV.
observed: Prefix caching consumes memory to store cached KV. It can reduce aggregate KV residency when many requests share a prefix, but it does not 'reduce memory capacity'; it trades cache memory for prefill compute and duplicate KV. The phrase is backwards.
evidence: A cached prefix occupies HBM; the benefit is avoiding duplicate KV and recomputation across requests. If the prefix is not reused, it is pure overhead.
root_cause: Resource trade-off described as a capacity reduction.
correction: Say 'Prefix caching trades cache memory for reduced prefill compute and, when prefixes are shared, reduced duplicate KV residency; it can also reduce effective capacity if hit rate is low.'
acceptance_test: The text states the memory cost and the hit-rate condition; no claim that prefix caching reduces physical memory capacity.

quoted_clause: so decode slots never sit idle
observed: Continuous batching reduces scheduler-induced idle slots but cannot guarantee no idle. Slots can be idle because no request is ready, KV capacity is exhausted, prefill is running, the scheduler enforces an SLO/admission policy, or the batch is limited by memory/communication.
evidence: The mechanism admits/evicts at each step; it does not create work. The chapter's own measurement section asks to track 'idle decode slots,' which contradicts 'never.'
root_cause: Mechanism benefit stated as a guarantee.
correction: Say 'can keep decode slots busier by refilling freed slots when requests are available; idle can still occur due to insufficient arrivals, KV capacity, prefill, or scheduling policy.'
acceptance_test: No 'never' claim; the text lists conditions under which idle remains and reconciles with the measurement section.

quoted_clause: while a long decode runs, the freed FLOPs are continuously refilled by new short requests
observed: Decode is described in the same chapter as bandwidth-bound. The resource freed by a finishing request is a decode slot and its share of memory-bandwidth demand, not 'FLOPs.' Using FLOPs here contradicts the resource model and can mislead about what continuous batching amortizes.
evidence: Continuous batching amortizes per-step weight reads across more sequences; it increases arithmetic intensity and bandwidth utilization. It does not primarily refill idle FLOPs.
root_cause: Resource terminology drift between compute and bandwidth.
correction: Say 'freed decode slots and memory-bandwidth capacity are refilled by new requests, amortizing the per-step weight reads.'
acceptance_test: The sentence uses the same resource terms as the chapter's mental model; no 'freed FLOPs' in a bandwidth-bound decode explanation.

quoted_clause: When a GPU is *idle* waiting, we reach for DP/CP (more work per GPU).
observed: CP splits the sequence dimension across GPUs; it does not give each GPU 'more work' in the sense of independent requests. It addresses per-GPU sequence/KV/attention capacity and introduces communication. DP adds independent work; CP redistributes one request's sequence.
evidence: The strategy table says CP splits the token sequence and communicates KV via ring. That is a capacity/latency trade, not an idle-GPU fill.
root_cause: Resource triangle mapping conflates DP and CP.
correction: Say 'DP adds independent work; CP addresses long-sequence/KV capacity by splitting the sequence, at the cost of communication.'
acceptance_test: The mental model maps each strategy to the resource it addresses; CP is not described as adding work per GPU.

quoted_clause: Sequence/context parallelism (CP) ... (Inference-centric; the serving analogue of training sequence parallelism.)
observed: The opening says 'context/pipeline partitioning and expert parallelism both appear in training too,' and only P/D has no training analogue. Calling CP 'inference-centric' and a 'serving analogue' of training sequence parallelism contradicts that taxonomy. CP/sequence parallelism is used in training as well.
evidence: The same section lists CP as a strategy and says context/pipeline partitioning appears in training. The parenthetical narrows it without explanation.
root_cause: CP conflated with a specific inference serving variant.
correction: Define CP as an axis used in both training and inference; if the book means an inference-specific context-partitioning variant, name it separately and state the training analogue.
acceptance_test: The taxonomy table and prose agree on which strategies have training analogues; CP is not both 'appears in training' and 'inference-centric' without qualification.

quoted_clause: PagedAttention and prefix caching both raise the effective KV packing; track it.
observed: PagedAttention improves KV packing by reducing external fragmentation/over-reservation. Prefix caching does not raise packing; it avoids duplicate prefill/KV for shared prefixes. It can improve effective capacity via sharing, but that is a different mechanism and depends on hit rate.
evidence: The chapter's own table lists PagedAttention's primary resource as memory capacity and prefix caching's as prefill FLOPs + memory. Measurement should distinguish them.
root_cause: Two different KV mechanisms collapsed into one metric.
correction: Say 'track KV block utilization/packing for PagedAttention and prefix-cache hit rate/shared-KV residency for prefix caching; do not use one packing metric for both.'
acceptance_test: Measurement section has separate metrics for block packing and prefix-cache hit rate; no claim that prefix caching raises packing.

quoted_clause: Serving both from one pool forces a compromise: batch for prefill and it slows decode; optimize for decode and prefill starves.
observed: This is true for a naive co-located scheduler without chunked prefill or phase-aware scheduling. Modern serving engines can chunk prefill and interleave it with decode, reducing the conflict. The sentence presents the trade-off as forced by co-location itself.
evidence: Chunked prefill exists precisely to interleave prefill chunks with decode; the book discusses it elsewhere. The conflict is scheduler-dependent, not a law of one pool.
root_cause: Scheduler implementation detail treated as a physical constraint.
correction: Qualify: 'Without chunked prefill or phase-aware scheduling, co-location forces a compromise...; chunked prefill can reduce the interference at the cost of latency/throughput trade-offs.'
acceptance_test: The claim is scoped to the scheduler assumption; the text mentions chunked prefill as a countermechanism.

quoted_clause: it pays off only when the workload outgrows a node and the two phases' resource conflicts become binding
observed: P/D disaggregation can be beneficial within a node if prefill/decode interference is severe, and it can be unhelpful after outgrowing a node if KV transfer or orchestration dominates. The 'only' is too strong and ties the decision to a topology threshold rather than measured phase interference.
evidence: The chapter's own condition is 'resource conflicts become binding'; that can happen at any scale. The node boundary is not the causal variable.
root_cause: Topology threshold substituted for bottleneck diagnosis.
correction: Say 'often premature for a single 8×H100 host at 10 rps; evaluate when measured phase interference or scaling limits bind, which may occur before or after crossing a node.'
acceptance_test: No 'only when outgrows a node' claim; the decision is tied to measured interference and KV-transfer cost.

quoted_clause: Speculative decoding is an optimization for bandwidth-bound decode, not a requirement
observed: Speculative decoding typically helps when decode is memory-bandwidth-bound and the target has spare compute, but it can hurt when decode is compute-bound, acceptance rate is low, draft cost is high, or batching already saturates compute. The sentence states a general condition without the acceptance-rate/compute-headroom caveats.
evidence: The mechanism trades extra draft/verification compute for fewer sequential target steps; the net effect depends on acceptance rate, draft/target cost ratio, batch size, and hardware balance.
root_cause: Mechanism condition compressed into a universal optimization label.
correction: Say 'typically helps memory-bandwidth-bound decode when acceptance rate is high and compute headroom exists; can hurt compute-bound or low-acceptance workloads; validate on the target workload.'
acceptance_test: The speculative-decoding discussion states acceptance rate, verification cost, draft cost, batch/concurrency, and hardware conditions; no unqualified 'optimization for bandwidth-bound decode.'

quoted_clause: A hybrid model can require both paged history and bounded recurrent state. A looped-depth model can require iteration-specific caches.
observed: The serving chapter introduces 'hybrid model,' 'looped-depth model,' 'early-exit interface,' and 'adaptive depth' without local definitions or cross-references. A reader who has not encountered these architectures cannot map them to the serving mechanisms.
evidence: The surrounding text discusses paged KV, prefix reuse, preemption, and speculative rollback; these new terms are not defined in the chunk.
root_cause: Advanced model-specific qualifications inserted into a general serving section without prerequisite support.
correction: Add one-sentence definitions and cross-references, or move the qualification to an appendix/advanced section. If retained, state which serving mechanism changes for each model type.
acceptance_test: Each term is defined or cross-referenced before use; a reader can explain why it changes cache/scheduling requirements.

quoted_clause: how they share the host's KV budget
observed: KV cache resides in GPU HBM, not host DRAM. In this book 'host' often means the 8-GPU server, but 'host's KV budget' can be read as CPU memory. The phrase blurs the memory hierarchy.
evidence: The chapter later uses '640 GB node memory' and 'GPU memory capacity.' The term should match.
root_cause: Host vs GPU HBM terminology drift.
correction: Say 'the node's HBM KV budget' or 'the GPU HBM KV budget.' Reserve 'host memory' for CPU DRAM.
acceptance_test: Search 'host's KV budget'; replace with HBM/node terminology where the KV cache is in GPU memory.

quoted_clause: the full 9.2K canonical input is ~1.29
observed: The value lacks a unit. The preceding calculation is in PFLOP, so the reader must infer 'PFLOP.'
root_cause: Unit elision.
correction: Write '~1.29 PFLOP.'
acceptance_test: The sentence includes the unit and matches the arithmetic.

quoted_clause: reports up to **525% throughput lift**
observed: A '525% lift' is ambiguous: +525% (6.25× baseline) vs 525% of baseline (5.25×). The text also does not state the baseline, workload, or whether the number is simulated vs real. The adjacent '+75% request count' has the same baseline ambiguity.
evidence: The source is a paper with specific evaluation conditions; the book's own evidence standard requires scope.
root_cause: Percentage-change wording not normalized.
correction: Write 'up to 6.25× the baseline throughput (+525%) in the paper's long-context simulation, and +75% completed requests on its Kimi workload; these are paper-specific, not portable.'
acceptance_test: The claim states baseline, multiplier, workload, and simulation/real distinction.

quoted_clause: These extreme sparsities ... are why expert-parallel and fused cross-expert comm kernels ... are increasingly central
observed: Sparsity is one driver, but EP is required because total expert parameters exceed a device and routing requires all-to-all; fused kernels address communication cost. The sentence makes sparsity the cause of EP centrality, which is too strong.
evidence: The same paragraph correctly says the memory-bound EP decision is made against total parameters, not active parameters. Total residency and routing communication, not sparsity alone, drive EP.
root_cause: Causal chain compressed; active-parameter sparsity conflated with total-expert residency.
correction: Say 'extreme sparsity makes active compute small relative to total residency, which, together with all-to-all routing cost, drives EP and fused communication kernels.'
acceptance_test: The causal claim distinguishes active compute, total residency, and routing communication.

quoted_clause: Within each node, the MoE active weights are small, so the team uses EP to shard experts + TP inside the node.
observed: The mini-case gives only total parameters (400B) and no active-parameter count, expert count, or per-node memory budget. 'Active weights are small' is asserted, not derived. EP is used to shard total experts; TP is used for the active dense/attention weights. The sentence conflates the two.
evidence: The preceding paragraph says the model is 400B MoE but does not state active parameters. Without that, the reader cannot verify the split.
root_cause: Unsupported assumption in a diagnostic mini-case.

quoted_clause: Server — one host with 1-8 GPUs, typically H100/H200, joined by NVLink/NVSwitch.

quoted_clause: Serves small models (up to ~7-13B at tight context)
observed: The 7-13B range is given without precision or quantization. A 13B FP16 model is ~26 GB of weights alone, which does not fit many single-GPU edge devices; the range is only plausible with quantization or a large-memory GPU.

quoted_clause: These three numbers locate the workload on the ladder objectively.
observed: The three numbers are a mix of measured residency, measured goodput, and a heuristic communication-fraction threshold (>~20%). Calling the placement 'objective' overstates the method; the communication threshold is explicitly illustrative.

quoted_clause: Most workloads never exceed one host's latency budget; the mistake is building a fleet before measuring whether traffic actually outgrows one host's capacity.
observed: The sentence switches from 'latency budget' to 'capacity' in the same claim. A workload can exceed a latency budget without exceeding capacity (e.g. SLO too tight), and vice versa. The common mistake is about capacity/goodput, not latency budget.
evidence: The parenthetical immediately discusses capacity at 40 rps peak. The intended metric is host capacity/goodput, not latency budget.
root_cause: Metric confusion in the common-mistakes item.
correction: Replace 'latency budget' with 'capacity/goodput ceiling' or split the two claims.
acceptance_test: The common-mistakes item uses one metric consistently and matches the parenthetical.

quoted_clause: C ≈ 17.5 gives at most 17 whole-context slots ... the unfloored 17.5-slot quotient gives ~2.03 req/s ... the ~3% gap is the fractional-slot rounding
observed: The text mixes a floored provisioning quotient (17) with an unfloored analytical quotient (17.5) and calls the resulting rate difference a '~3% gap' from fractional-slot rounding. The arithmetic is approximately right (17/8.6 ≈ 1.98; 17.5/8.6 ≈ 2.03; relative gap ≈ 2.9%), but the explanation is conceptually muddled: the gap is not merely rounding; it is the deliberate difference between a conservative integer-slot provisioning rule and an analytical fractional-slot screen. The same paragraph also uses 'at most 17 whole-context slots' and '17.5-slot quotient' without stating whether the per-slot KV footprint includes the ~300 generated output tokens or only the ~9,200 input tokens.
evidence: Recomputation: 17 / 8.6 = 1.9767 ≈ 1.98; 17.5 / 8.6 = 2.0349 ≈ 2.03; (2.0349 − 1.9767) / 2.0349 ≈ 2.86%, so '~3%' is numerically acceptable. However, the canonical workload is ~9,200 input + ~300 output tokens. If C ≈ 17.5 is computed at 9,200 tokens, then at 9,500 tokens the quotient becomes 17.5 × 9,200 / 9,500 ≈ 16.95, i.e. at most 16 whole-context slots, not 17. The chunk does not state the KV basis for C.
root_cause: The paragraph conflates three distinct quantities: analytical fractional-slot capacity, integer provisioning capacity, and request-rate ceiling. It also leaves the KV footprint basis implicit, so the reader cannot tell whether the 17-slot floor is conservative or optimistic once output tokens are included.
correction: State explicitly whether C ≈ 17.5 is computed for the full request sequence (input + output) or for input only. If it is input-only, recompute the whole-context slot count at the full sequence length and adjust the floor. Rewrite the gap sentence to say: 'The 17-slot provisioning floor and the 17.5-slot analytical screen differ by about 3% in rate; the floor is a conservative integer-slot rule, not a measurement.' Avoid calling the difference merely 'rounding' unless the KV basis is identical.
acceptance_test: The revised paragraph must (a) name the token basis for C, (b) show the full-sequence KV quotient if output tokens are included, (c) reproduce 17/8.6 ≈ 1.98 and 17.5/8.6 ≈ 2.03, and (d) explain the ~3% difference as a provisioning-vs-analysis choice rather than an unexplained rounding artifact.

quoted_clause: until then the candidate's status stays UNMEASURED ... [UNMEASURED] ... [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION][UNMEASURED]
observed: The chunk repeatedly uses [UNMEASURED] as a status label in the worksheet and in prose. The house evidence-label vocabulary defines status labels as [FACT], [DERIVED], [ASSUMPTION], [HYPOTHESIS], and [UNRESOLVED], plus [ANALYTICAL] on the third axis. [UNMEASURED] is not in that set. The chunk also combines it with valid labels, e.g. [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION][UNMEASURED], which makes the invalid label look like part of the formal taxonomy.
evidence: House convention: provenance [1P] [2 degree] [LAB] [ILLUSTRATIVE]; status [FACT] [DERIVED] [ASSUMPTION] [HYPOTHESIS] [UNRESOLVED]; plus [ANALYTICAL]. The chunk uses [UNMEASURED] in the table status column and in body text. No definition of [UNMEASURED] appears in the chunk.
root_cause: A local status word has been promoted to a bracketed evidence label without being added to the book's defined taxonomy. This is exactly the kind of terminology drift that makes evidence labels unreliable across chapters.
correction: Either replace [UNMEASURED] with an existing status label that expresses the intended meaning (likely [UNRESOLVED] for 'not yet measured' or [ASSUMPTION] for 'illustrative planning assumption'), or add [UNMEASURED] to the formal taxonomy in Ch 4 and Appendix A and define its scope. If retained, do not combine it with [ASSUMPTION] unless the axes are explicitly separated.
acceptance_test: A global search for '[UNMEASURED]' must return either zero hits or a definition in the Ch 4/Appendix A label table plus consistent use across all chapters. The worksheet status column must use only labels from the defined taxonomy.

quoted_clause: model capability is the goal (Ch4's Quality dimension), the constraint these deployment benchmarks do not measure; if capability fails its quality gate (Ch 12's candidate (c)), it becomes the binding constraint before any serving optimization.
observed: The sentence is grammatically and conceptually tangled. 'model capability is the goal ..., the constraint these deployment benchmarks do not measure' reads as an appositive that equates 'goal' with 'constraint', which is the opposite of the intended distinction. The clause 'if capability fails its quality gate ... it becomes the binding constraint' is also compressed: capability is not a constraint that 'fails'; a candidate fails the capability gate.
evidence: The surrounding argument distinguishes capability (quality) from deployment (SLO/performance). The sentence should say that capability is the quality gate, while deployment benchmarks measure the serving constraints that capability benchmarks do not. As written, a careful reader must reconstruct that distinction.
root_cause: Compression has collapsed two ideas—capability as a screening gate and deployment as a constraint measurement—into one clause with an unclear subject.
correction: Rewrite for example: 'Capability benchmarks answer whether the model clears the quality gate (Ch 4's Quality dimension). They do not measure the serving constraints—latency, throughput, cost, and behavior under our traffic—that deployment benchmarks must establish. If a candidate fails the capability gate (Ch 12's candidate (c)), no serving optimization can rescue it.'
acceptance_test: The revised sentence must clearly separate 'quality gate' from 'serving constraints' and must not imply that capability itself is a deployment constraint.

quoted_clause: The "4 chars ≈ 1 token" estimate can be 2-5× off for code/JSON/technical text (Ch6).
observed: The claim that the 4-chars-per-token heuristic can be '2-5× off' is stronger than the typical tokenization behavior for code/JSON/technical text. A 2× error means about 2 characters per token; a 5× error means about 0.8 characters per token. The latter is extreme for ordinary code/JSON and is not supported in the chunk. The sentence would be safer and more accurate as 'can be off by a factor of roughly 1.5–3×' or 'can be materially wrong' with a concrete example.
evidence: The heuristic is 4 characters/token. A 2× undercount implies 2 characters/token; a 5× undercount implies 0.8 characters/token. Code and JSON do tokenize worse than prose, but a 5× factor is an outlier, not a general expectation. The chunk provides no measurement or citation for the range.
root_cause: A useful warning has been overquantified into a range that is not defended and may not hold for typical code/JSON.
correction: Replace with a scoped statement such as: 'The 4-chars ≈ 1-token heuristic can be off by a factor of roughly 1.5–3× for code, JSON, and other punctuation-heavy text; measure with the model's tokenizer rather than extrapolating.' If the book has a measured example supporting 5×, cite it and state the exact text type.
acceptance_test: The revised claim must either cite a measured example for the upper bound or narrow the range to one the book can defend. A reader should not come away thinking 5× is a normal code/JSON tokenization error.

quoted_clause: Picking a serving stack with capability metrics — e.g. benchmarking a model's MMLU to choose serving hardware.
observed: This example is close to a straw man. A competent architect is unlikely to benchmark MMLU in order to choose serving hardware; the more plausible error is choosing a model or serving stack from a leaderboard without measuring the target workload. The adjacent example—'taking the top-scoring MMLU model and assuming it will meet our SLO'—is the stronger and more realistic trap.
evidence: The section's own distinction is capability screening vs deployment selection. The first example conflates a capability metric with a hardware-selection metric in a way that is almost a category mistake, while the second example is a real deployment error.
root_cause: The first bullet tries to illustrate 'wrong tool' but chooses an implausibly naive action.
correction: Replace the first example with a realistic one, e.g. 'Choosing a serving configuration because the model tops a capability leaderboard, without measuring TTFT/goodput on the target hardware and traffic.' Or merge the two bullets into one stronger example.
acceptance_test: The revised example must describe an error a competent team could plausibly make under schedule or procurement pressure, not a trivial category mistake.

quoted_clause: The scenario's 40 req/s peak and assumed 8.6-second execution time imply about 344 executing requests fleet-wide, not resident requests on one host.
observed: The phrase 'executing requests' is ambiguous. By Little's law, 40 req/s × 8.6 s ≈ 344 is the average number of requests in the system, including any queueing if 8.6 s is end-to-end residence time. If 8.6 s is pure execution/service time, 344 is the average number executing; if it includes queueing, 344 is the average resident population. The text says 'executing' and then contrasts with 'resident requests on one host', which blurs the distinction it is trying to make.
evidence: Little's law: L = λW. With λ = 40 req/s and W = 8.6 s, L ≈ 344. The interpretation of L depends on whether W is service time or residence time. The chunk does not define which 8.6 s is being used here, although earlier it calls it 'execution time'.
root_cause: The canonical 8.6 s value is being used as both a service-time input to per-host residency and a fleet-wide Little's-law population without restating the boundary.
correction: State the boundary explicitly: 'If 8.6 s is the mean end-to-end residence time, Little's law gives about 344 requests in the fleet on average; if it is pure execution time, 344 is the average number executing and the resident population is larger by the queueing term.' Then use the same definition consistently in the mini-case.
acceptance_test: The revised text must define whether 8.6 s is service time or residence time at each use, and the 344 figure must be labeled accordingly.
